rationale: Defines 'major ICT-related incident', one of the triggers that DORA 6(5) names; the answer can name the trigger without the definition, and the need does not use the term.
The duty to have 'a sound, comprehensive and well-documented ICT risk management framework': it is what gets reviewed, but it states neither the frequency nor the triggers.

The framework 'shall be documented and reviewed at least once a year' and 'upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents, and following supervisory instructions or conclusions derived from relevant digital operational resilience testing or audit processes': the cycle and the triggers asked for.
Same 'at least yearly' wording, but its object is 'the risk scenarios impacting them', not the ICT risk management framework: it applies to the bank and still answers neither question.

It requires entities to 'regularly review their ICT business continuity policy and ICT response and recovery plans', a duty the lead-in places 'As part of their comprehensive ICT risk management': it reviews a part of the framework, not the framework, and states neither a frequency nor an extra trigger for the framework review, so it is not 3 or 2. It is a different obligation rather than the same rule in a parallel regime, so the twin rule does not force a 0, and since a calendar for the framework can reasonably draw on the reviews of its parts it is not 'definitely not relevant' (section 2, scope check) but useful context a correct answer can leave out: grade 1.

It requires 'post ICT-related incident reviews after a major ICT-related incident disrupts their core activities', analysing 'the causes of disruption': this reviews the incident, not the framework, so the answer on the framework's cycle and triggers is correct and complete without it (not 2). Because it fires on a major ICT-related incident and its output is 'required improvements to the ICT operations or within the ICT business continuity policy referred to in Article 11', a part of the ICT risk management, it is not 'definitely not relevant' as section 2 requires for a 0, but useful context a correct answer can leave out: grade 1.
A mandate for standards on 'the content and format of the report on the review of the ICT risk management framework': it does not fix the frequency or the triggers asked for.

The simplified framework is 'reviewed periodically and upon the occurrence of major ICT-related incidents', but it is the framework 'referred to in paragraph 1, second subparagraph, point (a)', and 16(1) lists small and non-interconnected investment firms, exempted payment, e-money and credit institutions and small IORPs: a mid-sized bank is none of them.
The lead-in 'this Regulation applies to the following entities:' turns point (b) into the scope rule; without it point (b) is a bare list item.
'payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366': the exempt small payment business is covered by DORA.

'electronic money institutions, including electronic money institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2009/110/EC' has the same construction but reaches e-money institutions; the need states an exemption for small payment institutions.
Entities in points (a) to (t) 'shall collectively be referred to as financial entities': a name the answer does not need.

The exclusions ('This Regulation does not apply to:') to which paragraph 1 is subject; its points name fund managers, certain insurers, small IORPs, persons exempted under the investment-services directive, small insurance intermediaries and post office giro institutions, none of which the facts make the business, so it cannot change the answer.

Point (d) takes out of DORA only 'natural or legal persons exempted pursuant to Articles 2 and 3 of Directive 2014/65/EU', an investment-services exemption, while the need states a business under the exemption for small payment institutions, so the facts rule this exclusion out. Under the exceptions rule ('1 when the facts of the need rule them out') it is a 1, not a hard negative: it is an exclusion from the very scope the need asks about, and useful contrast because it is the case where an exemption does keep a person outside DORA, which is the founder's assumption.

The option lets Member States exclude only 'entities referred to in Article 2(5), points (4) to (23), of Directive 2013/36/EU', and DORA:16.1 lists 'institutions exempted pursuant to Directive 2013/36/EU' apart from 'payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366', so the facts of the need rule this derogation out. Under the exceptions rule ('1 when the facts of the need rule them out') it is a 1 rather than a 0: a scope derogation the answer checks and sets aside, useful context for a founder who relies on a national exemption, which a correct and complete answer can leave out.
Defines 'payment institution' by reference to Directive (EU) 2015/2366; DORA 2(1)(b) names the exempted ones expressly, so the answer does not depend on this definition.

The derogation applies on the stated facts ('Articles 5 to 15 of this Regulation shall not apply to ... payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366'), but it presupposes that the business is within DORA and only lightens its ICT risk management regime, so it cannot change the answer to whether the business is covered 'at all', and the exceptions rule gives 2 only to a derogation that 'would change the answer'. The extent of the obligations is not asked, so this is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out (grade 1), not a node without which the answer would be wrong or incomplete.
Names the competent authority 'for payment institutions, including payment institutions exempted pursuant to Directive (EU) 2015/2366': it confirms coverage, but the answer stands on Article 2.
A 'payment institution' is one 'granted authorisation in accordance with Article 11': it explains why DORA has to name exempted payment institutions separately, but the answer can leave it out.

Member States may exempt persons providing payment services 'from the application of all or part of the procedure and conditions': it is the exemption the founder uses, and the need already describes it in those terms, so the mapping is obvious.
Exempted persons 'shall be treated as payment institutions': it supports the reading of DORA's 'payment institutions exempted', which DORA 2(1)(b) states by itself.
The exemption of persons 'providing only the payment service as referred to in point (8) of Annex I' is the account-information exemption, not the small payment institution exemption the need states.
Custody and administration is 'the safekeeping or controlling, on behalf of clients, of crypto-assets': the need already says 'keeps its customers' tokens in custody', so the mapping is obvious.
The 'register of positions' opened in the name of each client: background to the statement, not the frequency or the request.

'A summary of the custody policy shall be made available to clients at their request in an electronic format': it applies to custodians, but it concerns the custody policy, not a statement of the crypto-assets held.

Custodians 'shall provide their clients, at least once every three months and at the request of the client concerned, with a statement of position of the crypto-assets recorded in the name of those clients'.
Information 'about operations on crypto-assets that require a response from those clients': other client reporting, which a correct answer can leave out.

'periodic statements ... of the portfolio management activities carried out on their behalf' bind providers 'providing portfolio management'; even if the exchange also managed portfolios, that statement is about the activities, not the crypto-assets it holds in custody.

'The periodic statement referred to in the first subparagraph ... shall be provided every three months': the same figure for the portfolio-management statement, not for the custody statement asked for.

'A person shall not provide crypto-asset services, within the Union, unless' authorised: 61(1) disapplies 'the requirement for authorisation under Article 59', so the answer needs the rule it refers to.

The point only names the route the firm lacks ('authorised as crypto-asset service provider in accordance with Article 63'), which the need already presupposes ('without an EU authorisation'), and the exclusive-initiative exemption (MiCA Art. 61(1)) itself names the Article 59 authorisation requirement it disapplies, so neither question is answered wrongly or incompletely without this point. It is not a definition, condition, exception or lead-in, and under the whole-article reference rule a cross-reference 'never adds qrels by itself': useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out, grade 1.

A non-provider shall not 'issue marketing communications' suggesting that it is a crypto-asset service provider: it may bear on the emails depending on their content, which the need does not give; context.
Freedom to 'provide crypto-asset services throughout the Union' belongs to authorised crypto-asset service providers; the need states that the firm has no MiCA authorisation.
Where a client 'initiates at its own exclusive initiative' the service of a third-country firm, 'the requirement for authorisation under Article 59 shall not apply': the answer to the first question.

A firm that 'solicits clients or prospective clients in the Union, regardless of the means of communication used for the solicitation, promotion or advertising' does not serve at the client's own initiative: a condition that changes both answers.
Solicitation counts 'notwithstanding any contractual clause or disclaimer': it reinforces the condition without changing the answer.
The client's own exclusive initiative does 'not entitle a third-country firm to market new types of crypto-assets or crypto-asset services to that client': the answer to the email question.
A mandate for guidelines on 'the situations in which a third-country firm is deemed to solicit clients': Article 61 itself answers both questions, so it does not fix the element asked for.

The notification by 'A crypto-asset service provider that intends to provide crypto-asset services in more than one Member State' presupposes an authorised provider with a home Member State; the firm has no MiCA authorisation.
Defines 'crypto-asset service provider': the need's 'crypto exchange authorised under MiCA' maps to it obviously; it says nothing about transfer data.
Transfer services move crypto-assets 'from one distributed ledger address or account to another': it names the activity, not the data that must accompany it.
Procedures 'to comply with the provisions of national law transposing Directive (EU) 2015/849': it points to anti-money-laundering law, but states no data that must travel with a transfer.
Transfer service providers 'shall conclude an agreement with their clients': the only MiCA duty on transfer services, about the client agreement, not the transfer data.
'the identity of the parties to the agreement' is a term of the client agreement under 82(1), not information that must accompany each transfer; no reading of the facts makes it so.

Under Article 82 ('Providing transfer services for crypto-assets on behalf of clients') and the lead-in of paragraph 1 on the agreement the provider concludes with its clients, the node only makes 'a description of the modalities of the transfer service provided' a term of that agreement. It states no information about the sender or the recipient that must accompany a transfer, and it is not a definition, condition or exception that could change that answer, so it fails grades 3 and 2; sharing the topic of transfers is not the 'useful context' of grade 1. Scope check: the actor of the lead-in can be the exchange in the need, and no unstated fact turns a term of the client agreement into information accompanying each transfer, so the node is definitely not relevant and takes grade 0 (section 2, hard negatives and the scope check).
Guidelines on transfer 'procedures and policies, including the rights of clients': it does not say that the data asked for are fixed there.

The node says PSD2 'Articles 28, 29 and 30 shall be without prejudice to the obligation of competent authorities ... to supervise or monitor the compliance' with Directive (EU) 2015/849 and Regulation (EU) 2015/847. It binds supervisors, imposes nothing on the exchange and states no information about the sender or the recipient. Its mention of 'Article 22(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/847' is cited for that supervisory duty and only marks where to look, since 'A cross-reference never adds qrels by itself' (section 2, references to whole articles). Scope check: even if the exchange also came within those PSD2 articles, the node would still state nothing that must accompany a transfer, so it is definitely not relevant and takes grade 0 (hard negatives and the scope check).

Under 45(1) the provider gives its own user 'a specification of the information or unique identifier to be provided by the payment service user': information from provider to user before a payment, not data that travel with a transfer, whatever the asset.
Under 57(1) the payer's provider gives the payer, after the debit, 'information relating to the payee': information returned to the payer, not data that travel with a transfer.
DORA applies to 'crypto-asset service providers as authorised under' MiCA: context, since the need asks what the policy must contain under the crypto rules.
Sets the DORA 'comprehensive ICT business continuity policy' within the ICT risk management framework: part of the referred Article 11, context for the MiCA policy.
DORA's own aims for the ICT business continuity policy ('aiming to:'); the need asks what the policy must achieve under the crypto rules, which MiCA states.

The node requires entities to 'implement associated ICT response and recovery plans' and, for non-microenterprises, 'independent internal audit reviews', but the crypto rule quoted in the record already names this plan ('ICT response and recovery plans set up pursuant to Articles 11 and 12') together with its aims, so under the whole-article reference rule ('marks where to look, not what is relevant') the answer is neither wrong nor incomplete without this node. The audit requirement concerns the plans themselves, not what the policy must contain or aim at, so the node is useful context that a correct and complete answer can leave out: grade 1.

'put in place, maintain and periodically test appropriate ICT business continuity plans' sets up and tests the plan, but the need asks only which plans the policy must include and what it must aim at, and the crypto rule names 'ICT business continuity plans' itself. Under the whole-article reference rule a correct and complete answer can leave this node out, so it is useful context: grade 1.
A business impact analysis 'as part of the overall business continuity policy': a DORA element of the policy, not one the crypto rules name; context.
Testing the plans 'at least yearly': the plans named by MiCA must be tested, but the need does not ask how often; context.

The lead-in 'For the purpose of ensuring the restoration of ICT systems and data with minimum downtime, limited disruption and loss ... shall develop and document:' belongs to the referred Article 12 and echoes the recovery aim, but no part of Article 12 is needed to say which plans the policy must include or what it must aim at. The clause 'ambiguous when it cannot be told which part is needed' therefore does not arise, and the node is useful context: grade 1.

'restoration and recovery procedures and methods' are procedures behind recovery, not one of the plans the crypto rule requires the policy to include (it names only 'ICT business continuity plans' and 'ICT response and recovery plans'), and the answer is complete without them. Under the whole-article reference rule this is useful context, grade 1, and it is not ambiguous because the answer needs no part of Article 12.
Backup systems, and periodic testing of backup and restoration procedures: part of the referred Article 12, not needed to say which plans the policy includes.

Business continuity plans under the simplified framework of the entities listed in 16(1), which names small investment firms, exempted payment, e-money and credit institutions and small IORPs, not a crypto-asset service provider.
Defines 'crypto-asset service provider': the need's 'crypto exchange authorised under MiCA' maps to it obviously.

The same continuity wording, but 'Issuers of asset-referenced tokens shall establish a business continuity policy': the need is about a crypto exchange's policy, and nothing says it issues such tokens.
The general duty to 'ensure continuity and regularity in the performance of their crypto-asset services': the policy's content is stated in the second subparagraph.

Providers 'shall establish a business continuity policy, which shall include ICT business continuity plans as well as ICT response and recovery plans set up pursuant to Articles 11 and 12' of DORA 'that aim to ensure ... the preservation of essential data and functions and the maintenance of crypto-asset services' or their timely recovery.

Providers 'operating a trading platform' must keep trading systems 'subject to effective business continuity arrangements': a crypto exchange may operate one, so it is potentially useful context, but it is a separate duty from the policy.

Ten business days apply to 'a request for a refund'; 77(1) limits those requests to 'the refund referred to in Article 76 of an authorised payment transaction', and under 64(1) a transaction is authorised 'only if the payer has given consent': a second charge of the same card payment had no consent.
Procedures for complaints 'to the competent authorities' about alleged infringements: the need states that she complained to her provider, and this node sets no reply deadline for the provider.
Providers must have 'adequate and effective complaint resolution procedures': context, no deadline.
Reply 'at the latest within 15 business days of receipt of the complaint'; 'In exceptional situations' beyond the provider's control, a holding reply, and the final reply within 35 business days.
Member States may keep or introduce rules 'more advantageous to the payment service user': a derogation that can shorten the deadline, and the need names no Member State.

The node puts a duty on the same provider for the same kind of dispute ('shall inform the payment service user about at least one ADR entity which is competent to deal with disputes concerning the rights and obligations arising under Titles III and IV'). The need does not say whether the reply comes late or leaves her unsatisfied, and on a reasonable reading of those open facts this is potentially useful context, so the scope check rules out a 0, which is kept for 'definitely not relevant', never 'probably not relevant'. It states no reply deadline and no case in which the reply may take longer, so a correct and complete answer can leave it out: grade 1, not 2.
Member States must establish 'ADR procedures for the settlement of disputes': a different channel, with no deadline for the provider's reply.

A direct debit is 'initiated by the payee on the basis of the consent given by the payer to the payee': it confirms that the signed form is consent, but the need already uses the term in its legal sense.
A transaction 'is considered to be authorised only if the payer has given consent': the signed mandate is that consent, so the debit is authorised; the need makes this evident, context.
Consent 'may also be given via the payee': supports that signing the gym's form is consent; context.

Rectification of 'an unauthorised or incorrectly executed payment transaction' within 13 months: she signed a mandate that 'did not state a fixed amount', so the larger debit is within her consent (64(1), 64(2)) and was executed as ordered.
The next-business-day refund applies 'in the case of an unauthorised payment transaction'; the debit was authorised by the signed mandate, which fixed no amount.

'a payer is entitled to a refund ... of an authorised payment transaction which was initiated by or through a payee ... if both of the following conditions are met': the right exists despite the signed mandate.

Read with the Article 76(1) lead-in ('if both of the following conditions are met'), 'the authorisation did not specify the exact amount of the payment transaction when the authorisation was made' is one of two cumulative conditions of the refund right. The right itself ('a payer is entitled to a refund ... of an authorised payment transaction') is stated in the lead-in; section 2 grades a condition 2 when it 'can apply to the need and would change the answer', and here the need's form 'did not state a fixed amount' and without this condition there is no refund. The need asks whether she can get the money back, not for a list of conditions, so the list clause does not raise a single condition to 3.

Read with the same lead-in ('if both of the following conditions are met'), 'the amount of the payment transaction exceeded the amount the payer could reasonably have expected taking into account the previous spending pattern' is the second cumulative condition of the refund right, not the right itself. It can apply to the need ('a much larger monthly amount than usual') and would change the answer if it were not met, so section 2 grades it 2 ('an exception, condition or derogation that can change the answer'); the need asks a yes or no question about the right, not for the list of conditions, so the list clause does not make it a 3.
The payer bears 'the burden of proving such conditions are met' on request: practical detail.
The refund is 'the full amount': detail of the refund, not whether she gets it.

'for direct debits as referred to in Article 1 of Regulation (EU) No 260/2012, the payer has an unconditional right to a refund within the time limits laid down in Article 77': the need does not exclude such a debit, so this answers it directly on that branch.
A framework contract may provide that 'the payer has no right to a refund where': the need does not say where she gave consent, so the exception can apply and would change the answer.
Exception condition: consent given 'directly to the payment service provider'; open on the facts.
Exception condition: information on the future transaction provided 'for at least 4 weeks before the due date'; open on the facts.
For direct debits 'in currencies other than euro', Member States may offer more favourable rights: context.
The payer 'can request the refund ... for a period of 8 weeks from the date on which the funds were debited': about six weeks later, she still can.
Within 10 business days the provider refunds or justifies a refusal: how the bank responds, which the need no longer asks; context.
The right to refuse 'shall not apply' to the unconditional refund of 76(1) fourth subparagraph: it confirms that branch, which 76(1) already states as 'unconditional'; context.
'ICT third-party service provider' means 'an undertaking providing ICT services': the vendor running the core banking platform obviously is one, and no other category is plausible.
Defines 'ICT services'; the core banking platform obviously is one; not needed for the answer.

The lead-in 'Financial entities shall ensure that contractual arrangements on the use of ICT services may be terminated in any of the following circumstances:' turns points (a) to (d) into termination situations.
Situation: 'significant breach by the ICT third-party service provider of applicable laws, regulations or contractual terms'.
Situation: circumstances found in monitoring 'deemed capable of altering the performance of the functions provided through the contractual arrangement', including material changes.
Situation: the provider's 'evidenced weaknesses pertaining to its overall ICT risk management'.
Situation: 'where the competent authority can no longer effectively supervise the financial entity' because of the arrangement.
Exit strategies must take into account 'the termination of contractual arrangements ... under any of the circumstances listed in paragraph 7': it refers back to the answer; context.
Lead-in of the minimum contract content ('shall include at least the following elements:'); only point (h) concerns termination, and it is context, so the lead-in is too.

Access, recovery and return of data 'in the event of the termination of the contractual arrangements': what happens on termination, not when; context for someone reviewing the right to end the contract.
The contract must include 'termination rights and related minimum notice periods': it requires termination rights but names no situation; context.

The Lead Overseer assesses a critical provider's portability mechanisms 'which ensure an effective exercise of termination rights by the financial entities': the need does not say whether the vendor is critical; if it is, this is useful context, never the answer.

The node only obliges the Lead Overseer to 'inform the critical ICT third-party service provider of the consequences of such opposition, including the possibility' that authorities require termination, so even if the vendor were critical it would not itself state a situation in which the bank must be able to end the contract, and a complete answer can leave it out (grade 1, section 2). The need leaves open whether the vendor is critical, so the scope check rules out a 0 and makes it potentially useful context; no reading raises it above 1, so its grade is settled and it is not ambiguous.

Unlike a notice, this is the operative power: competent authorities 'may require financial entities to terminate, in part or completely, the relevant contractual arrangements concluded with the critical ICT third-party service providers', which adds a situation in which the bank must be able to end the contract only if the vendor is critical and only if the need's 'must be able to end' covers termination ordered by an authority, not just the circumstances the contract itself must allow. The need settles neither the vendor's status nor that reading, so the grade (1, or 2 or more) depends on interpretation and its applicability cannot be settled: ambiguous under the scope check and section 4, with grade 1 recorded.

Outsourcing agreements must give 'crypto-asset service providers the right to terminate': under 73(1) this binds crypto-asset service providers that outsource, and the need is about a bank's core banking contract.

A periodic penalty payment that the Lead Overseer imposes 'to compel the critical ICT third-party service provider': under 35(1) these powers are 'in respect of the critical ICT third-party service providers', not an insurer fined by its national supervisor.

'up to 1 % of the average daily worldwide turnover of the critical ICT third-party service provider': a ceiling of the Lead Overseer's powers over critical providers (35(1)), not a fine on an insurer by its national supervisor.
The authority 'for insurance and reinsurance undertakings' is the one designated under Directive 2009/138/EC: it identifies the national supervisor, which the need already names; context.
Competent authorities 'shall have all supervisory, investigatory and sanctioning powers necessary': the power exists, but no amount.

'Member States shall lay down rules establishing appropriate administrative penalties and remedial measures': it states where the maximum is fixed (national law); without it an answer could take a DORA figure that does not apply.
Penalties must be 'effective, proportionate and dissuasive': a standard, not an amount.
The lead-in by which authorities get 'the power to apply at least the following administrative penalties or remedial measures': it turns point (c) into a power.
'adopt any type of measure, including of pecuniary nature': the basis for a fine, stated without any amount; needed for a complete answer.
Criteria for 'the type and level' of a penalty: how a fine is sized within national law, not its maximum.

Article 52(1) lets Member States 'decide not to lay down rules for administrative penalties or remedial measures for breaches that are subject to criminal penalties'. That decides whether a supervisory fine exists at all, not how high it can go, and the need assumes that 'the company's national supervisor fined it', so the facts of the need rule the derogation out. Under section 2 (exceptions, conditions and derogations: '1 when the facts of the need rule them out') it is useful context on criminal exposure for the board briefing, so it is a 1, not a 2 and not a 0.
'maximum administrative fines of at least' for legal persons apply to the MiCA infringements listed in 111(1); an insurer's shortfall under DORA is not one of them.
'3 % of the average daily turnover' is the amount of periodic penalty payments that EBA imposes under 132(1); nothing in the need involves EBA or MiCA.
Penalties for 'infringements of the national law transposing this Directive', the payment services directive; the need is about an insurer falling short of DORA.
